paras: The killing of Thomas Williams was the shooting death of a Black farmer near Ocklocknee, in Thomas County, Georgia, on the night of Friday, August 28, 1903, after unknown parties called him out of his house. A coroner's jury attributed his death to parties unknown, while his wife accused a young white man who was said to have an alibi. The Savannah Morning News reported the killing chiefly as the cause of a possible "race war" in the county.

Williams lived four miles northeast of Ocklocknee, a town twelve miles north of Thomasville. About 9 o'clock on Friday night he was called out of his house by "unknown parties"; a few moments later shots were heard. His wife found him dying a short distance from the house.

The coroner's jury returned a verdict that Williams died "by the hands of parties unknown." His wife nonetheless accused "a well known young white man of Ocklocknee," who, according to the dispatch, was able to prove a complete alibi; no arrest is reported.

Many Black residents attended the funeral, where some complained and one was reported to have said that "the trouble had not yet started." On Saturday night Williams' brother bought 159 cartridges at an Ocklocknee hardware store, and other Black residents bought pistols and firearms. Every white family in the neighborhood was warned, and Black residents, especially workers at the turpentine stills, were "kept under a close watch." White residents said they would act only on the defensive, and Sunday passed quietly.

The only report found is a Thomasville dispatch dated August 31 that the Savannah Morning News printed on September 1 under the headline "Race War Possible in Thomas County." The dispatch called the killing "mysterious" but gave most of its space to the armed response of Black residents, describing their purchases as "suspicious actions" and the turpentine workers as "a turbulent class." It added that whites were in the majority and that any conflict "could have but one result." No coverage of the killing in the Black press or follow-up on the accusation or the threatened conflict was found.

reader.title: Killing of Thomas Williams
bases: A1 describes a Black farmer called from his house at night and shot by 'unknown parties', followed by a feared 'race war'; it names no mob, band or crowd, so the killing fits no group-violence category on this evidence.
Only one report, a Thomasville dispatch in the Savannah Morning News (A1), was found in either press.

accounts.label: Thomasville dispatch
accounts.gist: Williams was killed by unknown parties, as the coroner's jury found; his wife's accusation of a young white man was met by an alibi; the danger lay in armed Black residents, whom whites were watching while promising to act only defensively.

accounts.label: Williams' wife (as reported)
accounts.gist: She accused a well-known young white man of Ocklocknee of the killing.

framing.detail: Headline 'Race War Possible in Thomas County' and subhead 'Trouble Grew Out of Killing of Negro Farmer'; calls the killing 'mysterious', treats Black arms purchases as 'suspicious actions' and turpentine workers as 'a turbulent class', and says any conflict 'could have but one result'.

versions.value: A well-known young white man of Ocklocknee (Williams' wife)

conflicts.note: The same dispatch reports both and says the accused could prove a complete alibi; it does not say who vouched for the alibi or whether it was tested.

record_check.dossier: other: a night killing by 'unknown parties'; no mob or crowd is described
Supported: 'Friday night' before the Aug. 31 (Monday) dispatch
Single source: one white-press dispatch; no Black-press coverage found

info: Friday night, about 9 o'clock, before the dispatch dated Monday, Aug. 31, 1903 (i.e., Aug. 28, 1903)
Near Williams' house, four miles northeast of Ocklocknee, a Thomas county town twelve miles north of Thomasville
None against the victim is reported

sources.note: Thomasville dispatch of Aug. 31, 'Race War Possible in Thomas County': Williams called out at night and shot; coroner's jury 'parties unknown'; wife accuses a young white man said to have an alibi; Black residents buy arms, white families warned.
quotes: The trouble was started by the mysterious killing on Friday night of Thomas Williams, a negro farmer who lived four miles northeast of Ocklocknee.
He was called out of his house about 9 o'clock at night by unknown parties.
Williams' wife, however, accuses a well known young white man of Ocklocknee of the crime. He, however, is able to prove a complete alibi.
On Saturday night Williams' brother bought 159 cartridges in an Ocklocknee hardware store
The white people are in a majority in this district, and any conflict that should arise could have but one result.
The negroes are kept under a close watch, especially those of the turpentine stills, who are of a turbulent class.
